title: Sell Mineral Rights in Fairmont, WV
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Fairmont, WV | Marion County Seat
metaDescription: Fairmont, WV is Marion County's seat and its coal-and-gas courthouse record. We buy mineral rights, heir shares, and old flat-rate leases here directly.
heroLead: Fairmont is the Marion County seat, and its Clerk's office holds a deed record driven by two overlapping industries: coal, which built the city, and gas, which was leased alongside it for over a century.
intro: Marion County's coal legacy is inseparable from its mineral ownership picture. Deeds throughout Fairmont and the surrounding area routinely reserved coal to one party while treating oil and gas separately, sometimes in the same instrument, sometimes years apart. A mineral owner today may hold gas rights only, coal only, or both, depending entirely on what a great-grandparent's deed actually said.

We buy oil and gas mineral and royalty interests in and around Fairmont directly, reading the specific reservation language for your tract before making an offer, because assuming a standard split gets the estate wrong more often than it gets it right here.

sections.heading: Untangling generations of Fairmont-area heirs
paragraphs: Given the county's industrial history and population turnover, Fairmont-area mineral interests frequently show a dozen or more heirs across several branches of a family, some local, many scattered across the country. We buy individual shares and do the title work ourselves.

sections.heading: Coal-first county, gas-second ownership
paragraphs: Marion County's early economy ran on coal, and land transactions from that era reflect it: coal companies acquired the coal seam first, often leaving oil, gas, and surface rights with the original family or splitting them off in a later sale. Tracing a Fairmont-area gas interest means confirming it wasn't swept into an early coal-era conveyance by mistake or by broad reservation language.

sections.heading: New leasing activity in an established city
paragraphs: Marion County has continued to see Marcellus-era leasing activity even in and around a more developed city like Fairmont, where remaining undeveloped or lightly developed tracts can still be pulled into modern units.

sections.heading: Old flat-rate leases from the early gas era
paragraphs: Fairmont has some of Marion County's oldest gas leases on record, a number of them flat-rate, paying a fixed annual sum per well rather than a royalty percentage. West Virginia's statute sets a minimum one-eighth royalty upon conversion, but conversion isn't automatic. We check whether a Fairmont-area lease qualifies before pricing it.

faqs.question: How do I know if my Fairmont-area deed reserved coal, gas, or both?
faqs.answer: The specific reservation language in the recorded deed controls. We read the actual instrument rather than assuming a standard split applies.

faqs.question: Is my family's old Fairmont gas lease a flat-rate lease?
faqs.answer: Check whether it specifies a fixed dollar amount per well or a royalty percentage. We review the recorded lease to confirm which applies and whether it qualifies for statutory conversion.

faqs.question: Is there still active gas leasing in Marion County?
faqs.answer: Yes, though activity varies by specific tract and proximity to existing units. We check current status before making an offer.

faqs.question: How many heirs typically hold a Fairmont-area mineral interest?
faqs.answer: It varies, but interests with multiple generations of history commonly involve eight to fifteen or more co-owners.
